claim: Chronic pain affects between 11 and 40% of the population worldwide.
source: Chronic pain affects between 11 and 40% of the population worldwide (Cohen et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cohen et al., 2021.

claim: Only 30% of neuropathic pain patients achieve moderate (≥30%) relief using available treatments.
source: Neuropathic pain, which is pain arising from damage to the somatosensory nervous system, is particularly hard to treat with only 30% of patients achieving moderate (≥30%) relief using available treatments (Finnerup et al., 2015; Rosenberger et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Finnerup et al., 2015 and Rosenberger et al., 2020.

claim: Only 11% of analgesic drugs entering phase 1 trials are ultimately approved.
source: New treatments are needed but a meagre 11% of analgesic drugs entering phase 1 trials are ultimately approved (Hay et al., 2014), triggering debate about why basic science discoveries are not yielding improved clinical outcomes (Woolf, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hay et al., 2014.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in SCN9A cause congenital insensitivity to pain.
source: For instance, loss- or gain-of-function mutations in the gene SCN9A, which encodes the voltage-gated sodium channel NaV1.7, cause congenital insensitivity to pain (CIP) or painful neuropathies, respectively (Cox et al., 2006; Fertleman et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2004; for review see Dib-Hajj et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cox et al., 2006; Fertleman et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2004; and Dib-Hajj et al., 2013.

claim: Gain-of-function mutations in SCN9A cause painful neuropathies.
source: For instance, loss- or gain-of-function mutations in the gene SCN9A, which encodes the voltage-gated sodium channel NaV1.7, cause congenital insensitivity to pain (CIP) or painful neuropathies, respectively (Cox et al., 2006; Fertleman et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2004; for review see Dib-Hajj et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cox et al., 2006; Fertleman et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2004; and Dib-Hajj et al., 2013.

claim: Nociceptor-specific deletion of NaV1.7 abolishes acute and inflammatory pain in rodents.
source: In rodents, nociceptor-specific deletion of NaV1.7 abolishes acute and inflammatory pain (Nassar et al., 2004) but not neuropathic pain (Nassar et al., 2005; Minett et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nassar et al., 2004.

claim: Nociceptor-specific deletion of NaV1.7 does not abolish neuropathic pain in rodents.
source: In rodents, nociceptor-specific deletion of NaV1.7 abolishes acute and inflammatory pain (Nassar et al., 2004) but not neuropathic pain (Nassar et al., 2005; Minett et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nassar et al., 2005 and Minett et al., 2014.

claim: Global deletion of NaV1.7 blocks neuropathic pain in rodents.
source: Neuropathic pain is blocked by deleting NaV1.7 globally, including from sympathetic neurons (Grubinska et al., 2019; Minett et al., 2012), although not if the deletion is induced in adulthood (Shields et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Grubinska et al., 2019 and Minett et al., 2012.

claim: Global deletion of NaV1.7 induced in adulthood does not block neuropathic pain in rodents.
source: Neuropathic pain is blocked by deleting NaV1.7 globally, including from sympathetic neurons (Grubinska et al., 2019; Minett et al., 2012), although not if the deletion is induced in adulthood (Shields et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Shields et al., 2018.

claim: Insensitivity to pain associated with NaV1.7 loss-of-function mutations involves increased opioid signaling.
source: Furthermore, loss-of-function mutations in NaV1.7 do not consistently reduce nociceptor excitability (see Discussion) and the associated insensitivity to pain involves increased opioid signaling (MacDonald et al., 2021; Minett et al., 2015), consistent with naloxone's ability to restore pain sensitivity in CIP patients (MacDonald et al., 2021; Dehen et al., 1978).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to MacDonald et al., 2021; Minett et al., 2015; and Dehen et al., 1978.

claim: Naloxone can restore pain sensitivity in CIP patients.
source: Furthermore, loss-of-function mutations in NaV1.7 do not consistently reduce nociceptor excitability (see Discussion) and the associated insensitivity to pain involves increased opioid signaling (MacDonald et al., 2021; Minett et al., 2015), consistent with naloxone's ability to restore pain sensitivity in CIP patients (MacDonald et al., 2021; Dehen et al., 1978).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to MacDonald et al., 2021 and Dehen et al., 1978.

claim: No NaV1.7-selective drugs have passed phase 2 clinical trials.
source: Notwithstanding such reservations, several NaV1.7-selective drugs have been developed (Emery et al., 2016; Vetter et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2018) but none have yet passed phase 2 clinical trials (Kushnarev et al., 2020; Alsaloum et al., 2020; Eagles et al., 2022; Kitano and Shinozuka, 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kushnarev et al., 2020; Alsaloum et al., 2020; Eagles et al., 2022; and Kitano and Shinozuka, 2022.

claim: PF-05198007 prevents the flare response, indicating that at least some NaV1.7 channels are blocked.
source: This has been attributed to poor target engagement (Eagles et al., 2022; Mulcahy et al., 2019; Bankar et al., 2018; Kingwell, 2019) yet prevention of the flare response by PF-05198007, a NaV1.7-selective inhibitor, argues that at least some NaV1.7 channels are blocked (Alexandrou et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Alexandrou et al., 2016.

claim: CIP patients exhibit a normal flare response.
source: But CIP patients exhibit a normal flare response (McDermott et al., 2019), suggesting that their C fibers compensate for chronic loss of NaV1.7 channels.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to McDermott et al., 2019.

claim: CIP patients exhibit normal autonomic function.
source: But CIP patients exhibit normal autonomic function (Cox et al., 2006; McDermott et al., 2019), suggesting that their sympathetic neurons also compensate for chronic loss of NaV1.7 channels.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cox et al., 2006 and McDermott et al., 2019.

claim: Most small DRG neurons spike repetitively when depolarized by current injection.
source: Small dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons (soma diameter <25 µm) tend to spike repetitively when depolarized by current injection (Amir et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Amir et al., 1999.

claim: Most small nociceptors spiked repetitively when tested 2–8 hr after dissociation (DIV0).
source: In our sample, most small neurons genetically identified as nociceptors (see Materials and methods) spiked repetitively when tested 2–8 hr after dissociation (DIV0) or after 4–7 days in culture (DIV4-7), although the proportion of repetitively spiking neurons increased slightly over that interval (χ2=4.51, p=0.034, chi-square test; Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis (χ2=4.51, p=0.034).

claim: Most small nociceptors spiked repetitively when tested after 4–7 days in culture (DIV4-7).
source: In our sample, most small neurons genetically identified as nociceptors (see Materials and methods) spiked repetitively when tested 2–8 hr after dissociation (DIV0) or after 4–7 days in culture (DIV4-7), although the proportion of repetitively spiking neurons increased slightly over that interval (χ2=4.51, p=0.034, chi-square test; Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis (χ2=4.51, p=0.034).

claim: The proportion of repetitively spiking neurons increased slightly between DIV0 and DIV4-7.
source: In our sample, most small neurons genetically identified as nociceptors (see Materials and methods) spiked repetitively when tested 2–8 hr after dissociation (DIV0) or after 4–7 days in culture (DIV4-7), although the proportion of repetitively spiking neurons increased slightly over that interval (χ2=4.51, p=0.034, chi-square test; Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis (χ2=4.51, p=0.034).

claim: 100 nM TTX had no effect on the spiking pattern at DIV0.
source: Strikingly, 100 nM TTX had no effect on the spiking pattern at DIV0 but converted all but one neuron to transient spiking at DIV4-7.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 100 nM TTX converted all but one neuron to transient spiking at DIV4-7.
source: Strikingly, 100 nM TTX had no effect on the spiking pattern at DIV0 but converted all but one neuron to transient spiking at DIV4-7.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: TTX reduced firing rate only at DIV4-7 among neurons that spiked repetitively at baseline.
source: Amongst neurons that spiked repetitively at baseline, TTX reduced the firing rate and increased rheobase only at DIV4-7 (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: TTX increased rheobase only at DIV4-7 among neurons that spiked repetitively at baseline.
source: Amongst neurons that spiked repetitively at baseline, TTX reduced the firing rate and increased rheobase only at DIV4-7 (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: TTX reduced spike height at DIV0 and DIV4-7, but more so at DIV4-7.
source: TTX reduced spike height at DIV0 and DIV4-7, but more so at DIV4-7.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: There was a significant increase in capacitance between DIV0 and DIV4-7.
source: There was a significant increase in capacitance and leak conductance density between DIV0 and DIV4-7, but no change in resting membrane potential (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: There was a significant increase in leak conductance density between DIV0 and DIV4-7.
source: There was a significant increase in capacitance and leak conductance density between DIV0 and DIV4-7, but no change in resting membrane potential (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: There was no change in resting membrane potential between DIV0 and DIV4-7.
source: There was a significant increase in capacitance and leak conductance density between DIV0 and DIV4-7, but no change in resting membrane potential (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Only a small fraction of sodium current is TTX-sensitive at DIV0.
source: Consistent with current clamp data, voltage clamp recordings showed that only a small fraction of sodium current is TTX-S at DIV0, whereas nearly all sodium current was blocked by TTX at DIV4-7 (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by voltage clamp recordings shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Nearly all sodium current was blocked by TTX at DIV4-7.
source: Consistent with current clamp data, voltage clamp recordings showed that only a small fraction of sodium current is TTX-S at DIV0, whereas nearly all sodium current was blocked by TTX at DIV4-7 (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by voltage clamp recordings shown in Figure 1D.

claim: TTX-resistant channels play an important role in nociceptor excitability.
source: Previous studies suggested that TTX-R channels play an important role in nociceptor excitability (Caffrey et al., 1992; Renganathan et al., 2001; Rush et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Caffrey et al., 1992; Renganathan et al., 2001; and Rush et al., 2007.

claim: The contribution of TTX-resistant channels to nociceptor excitability diminishes after a few days in culture, with TTX-sensitive channels becoming dominant by DIV4.
source: Our initial results confirm this for DIV0 but show that their contribution diminishes after a few days in culture, with TTX-S channels becoming dominant by DIV4.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Excitability was remarkably stable between DIV0 and DIV4-7 despite reconfiguring of NaV channels.
source: Despite this reconfiguring of NaV channels, excitability was remarkably stable, consistent with previous work showing little change in excitability after axotomy despite large (but evidently counterbalanced) changes in TTX-R and TTX-S currents (Flake et al., 2004; Zhang et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citations to Flake et al., 2004 and Zhang et al., 1999.

claim: Similar changes in NaV channels develop in vivo following inflammation with consequences for drug efficacy assessed behaviorally.
source: We show later that similar changes develop in vivo following inflammation with consequences for drug efficacy assessed behaviorally (see Figure 8), suggesting the NaV channel reconfiguration described above is not a trivial epiphenomenon of culturing.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: 1 µM PF-24 abolished most of the sodium current at DIV0.
source: At DIV0, 1 µM PF-24 abolished most of the sodium current (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by voltage clamp recordings shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The PF-24-sensitive current had slow inactivation kinetics, like the TTX-resistant current.
source: The PF-24-sensitive current had slow inactivation kinetics, like the TTX-R current and unlike the fast TTX-S current in Figure 1D, and consistent with previous descriptions of NaV1.8 (Vijayaragavan et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations and a citation to Vijayaragavan et al., 2001.

claim: A-803467 had similar effects to PF-24 on sodium current at DIV0.
source: A different Nav1.8 antagonist, A-803467 (Jarvis et al., 2007), had similar effects (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and a citation to Jarvis et al., 2007.

claim: PF-24 converted 7 of 8 repetitively spiking neurons to transient spiking at DIV0.
source: In current clamp, PF-24 converted 7 of 8 repetitively spiking neurons to transient spiking and significantly reduced evoked spiking (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: PF-24 significantly reduced evoked spiking at DIV0.
source: In current clamp, PF-24 converted 7 of 8 repetitively spiking neurons to transient spiking and significantly reduced evoked spiking (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: PF-24 increased rheobase at DIV0.
source: It also increased rheobase and decreased spike height but did not affect resting membrane potential (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: PF-24 decreased spike height at DIV0.
source: It also increased rheobase and decreased spike height but did not affect resting membrane potential (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: PF-24 did not affect resting membrane potential at DIV0.
source: It also increased rheobase and decreased spike height but did not affect resting membrane potential (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: PF-24 had negligible effects when tested at DIV4-7.
source: PF-24 had negligible effects when tested at DIV4-7 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: NaV1.8 is the predominant NaV subtype at DIV0 and is necessary for repetitive spiking at that time point.
source: These results show that NaV1.8 is the predominant NaV subtype at DIV0 and is necessary for repetitive spiking at that time point.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing PF-24 effects at DIV0.

claim: Inclusion of NaV1.8 conductance was sufficient to generate repetitive spiking in the DIV0 computational model.
source: In this DIV0 model, inclusion of NaV1.8 conductance was sufficient to generate repetitive spiking (Figure 2D left).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 2D.

claim: 85% reduction in the NaV1.8 conductance converted spiking from repetitive to transient in the DIV0 model.
source: The necessity of NaV1.8 for repetitive spiking at DIV0 was also recapitulated: 85% reduction in the NaV1.8 conductance converted spiking from repetitive to transient (Figure 2D and Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 2D and Supplementary file 1A.

claim: Sodium current was significantly reduced by 30 nM PF-71 at DIV4-7.
source: In voltage clamp, sodium current was significantly reduced by 30 nM PF-71, and most of the remaining current was blocked by 1 µM ICA (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by voltage clamp recordings shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Most of the remaining sodium current after PF-71 application was blocked by 1 µM ICA at DIV4-7.
source: In voltage clamp, sodium current was significantly reduced by 30 nM PF-71, and most of the remaining current was blocked by 1 µM ICA (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by voltage clamp recordings shown in Figure 3A.

claim: PF-71 converted a significant proportion of neurons to transient spiking at DIV4-7.
source: In current clamp, each inhibitor (applied separately) converted a significant proportion of neurons to transient spiking and significantly reduced firing rate (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: ICA converted a significant proportion of neurons to transient spiking at DIV4-7.
source: In current clamp, each inhibitor (applied separately) converted a significant proportion of neurons to transient spiking and significantly reduced firing rate (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: PF-71 significantly reduced firing rate at DIV4-7.
source: In current clamp, each inhibitor (applied separately) converted a significant proportion of neurons to transient spiking and significantly reduced firing rate (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: ICA significantly reduced firing rate at DIV4-7.
source: In current clamp, each inhibitor (applied separately) converted a significant proportion of neurons to transient spiking and significantly reduced firing rate (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: NaV1.7 and NaV1.3 are both necessary for repetitive spiking at DIV4-7.
source: This argues that NaV1.7 and NaV1.3 are both necessary for repetitive spiking at DIV4-7.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing effects of PF-71 and ICA at DIV4-7.

claim: Inhibiting NaV1.7 increased rheobase at DIV4-7.
source: Inhibiting NaV1.7 increased rheobase, unlike inhibiting NaV1.3, and caused a stronger reduction in spike height (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Inhibiting NaV1.3 did not increase rheobase at DIV4-7.
source: Inhibiting NaV1.7 increased rheobase, unlike inhibiting NaV1.3, and caused a stronger reduction in spike height (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Inhibiting NaV1.7 caused a stronger reduction in spike height than inhibiting NaV1.3 at DIV4-7.
source: Inhibiting NaV1.7 increased rheobase, unlike inhibiting NaV1.3, and caused a stronger reduction in spike height (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Neither PF-71 nor ICA affected resting membrane potential at DIV4-7.
source: Neither affected resting membrane potential.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: NaV1.7 is the predominant NaV subtype at DIV4-7, but not the only one.
source: These results show that NaV1.7 is the predominant NaV subtype at DIV4-7, but not the only one.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing effects of PF-71 and ICA at DIV4-7.

claim: PF-71 had negligible effects when tested at DIV0.
source: PF-71 had negligible effects when tested at DIV0 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both NaV1.7 and NaV1.3 are required to produce repetitive spiking in the DIV4-7 computational model, meaning neither channel is individually sufficient.
source: We re-tuned our computational model to reproduce DIV4-7 data, with both NaV1.7 and NaV1.3 being required to produce repetitive spiking, meaning neither channel is individually sufficient (Figure 3D and Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 3D and Supplementary file 1A.

claim: Inserting a higher density of either NaV1.7 or NaV1.3 could produce repetitive spiking in the absence of the other subtype in the DIV4-7 model.
source: That said, inserting a higher density of either NaV1.7 or NaV1.3 could produce repetitive spiking in the absence of the other subtype (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), consistent with NaV1.7 and NaV1.3 also being interchangeable.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: NaV1.7 and NaV1.3 are interchangeable in the DIV4-7 model.
source: That said, inserting a higher density of either NaV1.7 or NaV1.3 could produce repetitive spiking in the absence of the other subtype (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), consistent with NaV1.7 and NaV1.3 also being interchangeable.
evidence: The claim is inferred from computational modeling results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The NaV1.8 current necessary for spiking in the DIV0 computer model can be replaced with NaV1.7 to restore repetitive spiking.
source: To verify that NaV1.7 and NaV1.8 currents are each sufficient to produce repetitive spiking, we tested whether the NaV1.8 current necessary for spiking in our DIV0 computer model could be replaced with NaV1.7, and whether the NaV1.7 current necessary for spiking in our DIV4-7 computer model could be replaced with NaV1.8. In both cases, repetitive spiking was restored after inserting the alternate current (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The NaV1.7 current necessary for spiking in the DIV4-7 computer model can be replaced with NaV1.8 to restore repetitive spiking.
source: To verify that NaV1.7 and NaV1.8 currents are each sufficient to produce repetitive spiking, we tested whether the NaV1.8 current necessary for spiking in our DIV0 computer model could be replaced with NaV1.7, and whether the NaV1.7 current necessary for spiking in our DIV4-7 computer model could be replaced with NaV1.8. In both cases, repetitive spiking was restored after inserting the alternate current (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Introducing virtual NaV1.7 after inhibiting native NaV1.8 restored repetitive spiking in all DIV0 neurons tested (3 of 3).
source: At DIV0 (left), inhibiting native NaV1.8 (with PF-24) converted neurons to transient spiking, but introducing virtual NaV1.7 reverted neurons to repetitive spiking (in 3 of 3 neurons tested).
evidence: The claim is supported by dynamic clamp experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Introducing virtual NaV1.8 after inhibiting native NaV1.7 restored repetitive spiking in all DIV4-7 neurons tested (4 of 4).
source: At DIV4-7, inhibiting native NaV1.7 (with PF-71) converted the neuron to transient spiking, but introducing virtual NaV1.8 reverted neurons to repetitive spiking (in 4 of 4 neurons tested).
evidence: The claim is supported by dynamic clamp experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Inserting virtual NaV1.8 after inhibiting native NaV1.8 restored repetitive spiking at DIV0.
source: Inserting virtual NaV1.8 after inhibiting native NaV1.8 also restored repetitive spiking, and likewise for NaV1.7 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), verifying that our virtual channels were equivalent to the native channels we aimed to replace.
evidence: The claim is supported by dynamic clamp experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Inserting virtual NaV1.7 after inhibiting native NaV1.7 restored repetitive spiking at DIV4-7.
source: Inserting virtual NaV1.8 after inhibiting native NaV1.8 also restored repetitive spiking, and likewise for NaV1.7 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), verifying that our virtual channels were equivalent to the native channels we aimed to replace.
evidence: The claim is supported by dynamic clamp experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the DIV0 model, subthreshold inward current was mediated mostly by NaV1.7 during the first spike but by NaV1.8 during the second and all subsequent spikes.
source: In the DIV0 model (Figure 5A and B), subthreshold inward current was mediated mostly by NaV1.7 during the first spike (left) but by NaV1.8 during the second and all subsequent spikes (right).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: The first spike at DIV0 is initiated using NaV1.7 whereas all subsequent spikes are initiated using NaV1.8.
source: We interpret this to mean that the first spike is initiated using NaV1.7 whereas all subsequent spikes are initiated using NaV1.8.
evidence: The claim is inferred from computational modeling results shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: The small NaV1.7 conductance at DIV0 quickly inactivates during the first spike and remains inactive during subsequent spikes.
source: This is explained by the small NaV1.7 conductance at DIV0 quickly inactivating during the first spike and remaining inactive during subsequent spikes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Inactivation of NaV1.7 after the first spike was reflected by an increase in voltage threshold between the first and second spike in the DIV0 model.
source: Inactivation of NaV1.7 after the first spike was reflected by an increase in voltage threshold between the first and second spike in the model (Figure 5A), which prompted us to check if the same increase was evident experimentally, which it was (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 5A and experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Voltage threshold increased between the first and second spike in DIV0 neurons experimentally.
source: Inactivation of NaV1.7 after the first spike was reflected by an increase in voltage threshold between the first and second spike in the model (Figure 5A), which prompted us to check if the same increase was evident experimentally, which it was (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: TTX caused a significant depolarizing shift in voltage threshold at DIV0.
source: This unanticipated simulation result also predicted that TTX should affect the voltage threshold of the first spike in DIV0 neurons despite not having other notable effects (see Figure 1); as predicted, TTX caused a significant depolarizing shift in voltage threshold at DIV0 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), further validating our model.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the DIV4-7 model, subthreshold inward current was mediated by NaV1.7 and NaV1.3 during the first spike and during all subsequent spikes, with NaV1.8 contributing little.
source: In the DIV4-7 model (Figure 5C and D), subthreshold inward current was mediated by NaV1.7 and NaV1.3 during the first spike (left) and during all subsequent spikes (right), with NaV1.8 contributing little.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: At DIV4-7, the first and second spikes differ significantly in their threshold, overshoot, and rise time.
source: At DIV4-7, the 1st and 2nd spikes differ in all measures (threshold: T7=7.613, p<0.001; overshoot: T7=−9.849, p<0.001; rise time: T7=5.979, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Differences between 1st and 2nd spike at DIV4-7 are significantly larger than differences at DIV0.
source: Statistical results (green) show that differences between 1st and 2nd spike at DIV4-7 are significantly larger than differences at DIV0 (threshold: T15=−3.847, p=0.002; overshoot: T15=7.922, p<0.001; rise time: T15=−5.617, p<0.001, unpaired t-tests), consistent with our computational model.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: NaV1.7 mRNA levels exceeded NaV1.8 mRNA levels at both DIV0 and DIV7.
source: NaV1.7 mRNA levels exceeded NaV1.8 mRNA levels at both DIV0 and DIV7.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Both NaV1.7 and NaV1.8 mRNA levels decreased between DIV0 and DIV7.
source: Both decreased between DIV0 and DIV7, but NaV1.8 more so, resulting in a significant decrease in the NaV1.8:NaV1.7 mRNA ratio.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: NaV1.8 mRNA decreased more than NaV1.7 mRNA between DIV0 and DIV7, resulting in a significant decrease in the NaV1.8:NaV1.7 mRNA ratio.
source: Both decreased between DIV0 and DIV7, but NaV1.8 more so, resulting in a significant decrease in the NaV1.8:NaV1.7 mRNA ratio.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Immunofluorescence for NaV1.8 was higher than for NaV1.7 at DIV0, and that ratio reversed at DIV7.
source: Immunofluorescence for NaV1.8 was higher than for NaV1.7 at DIV0, and that ratio reversed at DIV7 (Figure 6B), consistent with functional changes.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Cercosporamide significantly mitigated the decrease in NaV1.8 immunofluorescence and the increase in NaV1.7 immunofluorescence when applied to cultured neurons for 24 or 120 hr prior to measurements on DIV5.
source: Moreover, cercosporamide (10 µM), a potent inhibitor of the eukaryotic translation Initiation Factor 4E (eIF4E), significantly mitigated the decrease in NaV1.8 immunofluorescence and the increase in NaV1.7 immunofluorescence when applied to cultured neurons for 24 or 120 hr prior to measurements on DIV5 (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Translational regulation is crucial for changes in NaV1.7 and NaV1.8 protein levels between DIV0 and DIV7.
source: Beyond showing that their mRNA levels do not correlate well with NaV contributions to nociceptor excitability, reminiscent of some previous work (e.g. Berta et al., 2008), these results suggest that translational regulation is crucial, although membrane trafficking and other downstream processes likely also contribute (Dustrude et al., 2013; Yamane et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data and supported by citations to Berta et al., 2008; Dustrude et al., 2013; and Yamane et al., 2017.

claim: Inflammation increases NaV1.7 channel trafficking and membrane expression.
source: Inflammation increases NaV1.7 channel trafficking and membrane expression (Gould et al., 1998; Black et al., 2004; Liang et al., 2013; Akin et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gould et al., 1998; Black et al., 2004; Liang et al., 2013; and Akin et al., 2019.

claim: Inflammation caused nociceptors to become much more variable in their reliance on specific NaV subtypes.
source: Sample traces in Figure 7A show that inflammation caused nociceptors to become much more variable in their reliance of specific NaV subtypes, presumably because neurons innervating the inflamed paw experience greater effects of inflammation than neurons innervating other, non-inflamed sites.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Application of PF-71 to inhibit NaV1.7 converted 5 of 12 (42%) CFA neurons to transient spiking vs 0 of 9 (0%) of control neurons, which is a significantly higher proportion.
source: Specifically, application of PF-71 to inhibit NaV1.7 converted 5 of 12 (42%) CFA neurons to transient spiking vs 0 of 9 (0%) of control neurons, which is a significantly higher proportion (p=0.0451, Fisher exact test, Figure 7B, left)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Subsequent application of PF-24 to inhibit NaV1.8 converted only 1 of 7 (14%) of the remaining repetitive spiking CFA neurons to transient spiking vs 7 of 8 (88%) of control neurons, which is a significantly lower proportion.
source: whereas subsequent application of PF-24 to inhibit NaV1.8 converted only 1 of 7 (14%) of the remaining repetitive spiking CFA neurons to transient spiking vs 7 of 8 (88%) of control neurons, which is a significantly lower proportion (p=0.010, Figure 7B, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: PF-71 significantly affected resting membrane potential, rheobase, and spike height after CFA.
source: PF-71 also significantly affected resting membrane potential, rheobase, and spike height after CFA (Figure 7C), unlike in control neurons (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: NaV1.7 takes on greater responsibility for nociceptor excitability after inflammation.
source: Results above confirm that NaV1.7 takes on greater responsibility for nociceptor excitability after inflammation, which in turn predicts that PF-71 should reduce pain after inflammation but not under control conditions.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: PF-71 significantly reduced thermal sensitivity in CFA-inflamed mice without having any effect in control mice.
source: As predicted, PF-71 significantly reduced thermal (Figure 8A) and tactile (Figure 8B) sensitivity in CFA-inflamed mice without having any effect in control mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: PF-71 significantly reduced tactile sensitivity in CFA-inflamed mice without having any effect in control mice.
source: As predicted, PF-71 significantly reduced thermal (Figure 8A) and tactile (Figure 8B) sensitivity in CFA-inflamed mice without having any effect in control mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The inflammation-induced shift in NaV subtype expression is sufficient to cause a measurable change in drug efficacy assessed in vivo.
source: These results show that the inflammation-induced shift in NaV subtype expression, despite being variable (see Figure 7), is sufficient to cause a measurable change in drug efficacy assessed in vivo.
evidence: The claim is inferred from behavioral data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Epigenetic repression of NaV1.7 prevents/reverses hypersensitivity in inflamed and neuropathic mice without causing hyposensitivity in naïve mice.
source: Consistent with this, epigenetic repression of NaV1.7 prevents/reverses hypersensitivity in inflamed and neuropathic mice without causing hyposensitivity in naïve mice (Moreno et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Moreno et al., 2021.

claim: Genetic deletion of NaV1.7 reduces thermal and tactile sensitivity in naïve mice.
source: This is unlike genetic deletion of NaV1.7, which reduces thermal and tactile sensitivity in naïve mice (MacDonald et al., 2021), and with loss-of-function mutations in NaV1.7 that abolish pain in humans (Cox et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to MacDonald et al., 2021.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in NaV1.7 abolish pain in humans.
source: This is unlike genetic deletion of NaV1.7, which reduces thermal and tactile sensitivity in naïve mice (MacDonald et al., 2021), and with loss-of-function mutations in NaV1.7 that abolish pain in humans (Cox et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cox et al., 2006.

claim: Nociceptors can achieve similar excitability using different NaV channels.
source: Our results show that nociceptors can achieve similar excitability using different NaV channels.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Repetitive spiking depends on NaV1.8 shortly after dissociation and presumably under normal conditions in vivo.
source: Whereas repetitive spiking depends on NaV1.8 shortly after dissociation (Figure 2) and presumably under normal conditions in vivo, responsibility shifts to NaV1.7 and NaV1.3 after a few days in vitro (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and involves inference about in vivo conditions.

claim: Responsibility for repetitive spiking shifts to NaV1.7 and NaV1.3 after a few days in vitro.
source: Whereas repetitive spiking depends on NaV1.8 shortly after dissociation (Figure 2) and presumably under normal conditions in vivo, responsibility shifts to NaV1.7 and NaV1.3 after a few days in vitro (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Changes in NaV expression are due to translationally regulated changes.
source: This is due to translationally regulated changes in NaV expression (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Inflammation causes a similar shift in NaV dependence in vivo.
source: Inflammation causes a similar shift in vivo (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Acutely inhibiting a particular NaV is consequential (analgesic) only if that subtype is responsible for nociceptor excitability.
source: Importantly, acutely inhibiting a particular NaV is consequential (analgesic) only if that subtype is responsible for nociceptor excitability (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 8.

claim: NaV1.7 is not always necessary for nociceptor excitability depending on the expression level of NaV1.7 and other NaV subtypes.
source: This may explain why NaV1.7-selective drugs have not performed well in clinical trials (see Introduction) – because NaV1.7 is not always necessary for nociceptor excitability depending on the expression level of NaV1.7 and other NaV subtypes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data and clinical observations.

claim: Degeneracy – the ability of a biological system to achieve similar or even equivalent function using different components – complicates modulation of neuronal excitability.
source: For example, degeneracy – the ability of a biological system to achieve similar or even equivalent function using different components (Edelman and Gally, 2001) – complicates modulation of neuronal excitability by allowing changes in diverse ion channels to potentially subvert the therapeutic effect of a drug targeting a particular channel (Ratté and Prescott, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Edelman and Gally, 2001 and Ratté and Prescott, 2016.

claim: Neurons use diverse ion channel combinations to achieve similar function.
source: Contrary to the view that certain ion channels are uniquely responsible for certain aspects of neuronal function, neurons use diverse ion channel combinations to achieve similar function (Marder and Goaillard, 2006; O'Leary et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Marder and Goaillard, 2006 and O'Leary et al., 2014.

claim: Degeneracy is crucial for enabling excitability and other aspects of neuron physiology to be homeostatically regulated by adjusting ion channels in response to perturbations.
source: This degeneracy is crucial for enabling excitability and other aspects of neuron physiology to be homeostatically regulated by adjusting ion channels in response to perturbations (Drion et al., 2015; Mishra and Narayanan, 2022; Yang et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Drion et al., 2015; Mishra and Narayanan, 2022; and Yang et al., 2022.

claim: Degeneracy enables pathological changes in different ion channels to produce equivalent hyperexcitability.
source: Degeneracy also enables pathological changes in different ion channels to produce equivalent hyperexcitability (Drion et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Drion et al., 2011.

claim: Pacemaker activity in substantia nigra neurons can be mediated by NaV channels or by voltage-gated calcium channels.
source: Similar observations have been made in substantia nigra neurons, whose pacemaker activity can be mediated by NaV channels or by voltage-gated calcium channels, meaning TTX may or may not block their spiking (Drion et al., 2011; Puopolo et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Drion et al., 2011 and Puopolo et al., 2007.

claim: Similar interchangeability is evident for the burst firing of Purkinje neurons.
source: Similar interchangeability is evident for the burst firing of Purkinje neurons (Swensen and Bean, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Swensen and Bean, 2005.

claim: Degeneracy exists at the circuit level.
source: Degeneracy also exists at the circuit level (Knox et al., 2018; Prinz et al., 2004), where it allows differences in the intrinsic excitability of component neurons to be offset (and effectively hidden) by differences in synaptic weights (Grashow et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Knox et al., 2018; Prinz et al., 2004; and Grashow et al., 2010.

claim: The spinal dorsal horn circuit can achieve similar output using different synaptic weight combinations.
source: Relevant for pain processing, the spinal dorsal horn circuit can achieve similar output using different synaptic weight combinations (Medlock et al., 2022); specific neuron types may have a greater or lesser impact on circuit function depending on those weights.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Medlock et al., 2022.

claim: Ablating nociceptors abolishes acute and inflammatory pain but not neuropathic pain.
source: Indeed, ablating nociceptors abolishes acute and inflammatory pain but not neuropathic pain (Minett et al., 2014; Abrahamsen et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Minett et al., 2014 and Abrahamsen et al., 2008.

claim: NaV1.8 and NaV1.7 are similar but not identical in their gating properties.
source: Indeed, NaV1.8 and NaV1.7 are similar but not identical in their gating properties; for example, their voltage-dependencies partially overlap but the activation curve for NaV1.8 is right-shifted compared to NaV1.7 (Schild and Kunze, 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Schild and Kunze, 1997.

claim: NaV1.7 activates at voltages near threshold whereas NaV1.8 tends to activate at suprathreshold voltages.
source: Consequently, NaV1.7 activates at voltages near threshold whereas NaV1.8 tends to activate at suprathreshold voltages, during initiation and upstroke of the spike, respectively (Alsaloum et al., 2020; Bennett et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Alsaloum et al., 2020 and Bennett et al., 2019.

claim: NaV1.7 contributes to initiation of the first spike in DIV0 neurons, but because it inactivates more readily than NaV1.8, initiation of all subsequent spikes depends on NaV1.8.
source: We found that NaV1.7 contributes to initiation of the first spike in DIV0 neurons, but because it inactivates more readily than NaV1.8, initiation of all subsequent spikes depends on NaV1.8 (see Figure 5), which activates at perithreshold voltages because voltage threshold is high (depolarized) in the absence of NaV1.7.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and modeling results shown in Figure 5.

claim: The activation pattern for the first spike at DIV0 is consistent with Blair and Bean, 2002 who quantified the contribution of different NaV channels by recording pharmacologically isolated currents while varying the holding potential according to the spike waveform.
source: The activation pattern we report for the first spike at DIV0 is consistent with Blair and Bean, 2002 who quantified the contribution of different NaV channels by recording pharmacologically isolated currents while varying the holding potential according to the spike waveform.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Blair and Bean, 2002.

claim: Degeneracy at the cellular level must be considered when choosing drug targets at the molecular level.
source: Degeneracy at the cellular level must be considered when choosing drug targets at the molecular level.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the overall findings of the study.
